title: The Ancient Skeptics
objective: After this level you can explain how Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus balanced opposing arguments and suspended judgment in search of peace of mind.
summary: Pyrrhonian skeptics, recorded by Sextus Empiricus, set equal arguments against each other, suspended judgment and found tranquillity; critics said they could not act.

cards.headline: What if giving up on the answer brought you peace?
cards.body: Most philosophers chase answers. One school of Greek skeptics tried something stranger: weigh every argument against its opposite, stop judging, and see what happens to your worries.

cards.headline: Pyrrho, who wrote nothing
cards.body: The school is named after Pyrrho of Elis, who lived from about 365 to about 275 BCE. He wrote nothing, so we piece him together from other people’s reports. The fullest account comes centuries later, from Sextus Empiricus, probably of the second or third century CE, in his Outlines of Pyrrhonism.

cards.headline: The balancing skill
cards.body: Sextus describes the skeptic’s key ability: for every argument, find an equal and opposing argument. When the two weigh the same, like pans on a level scale, you suspend judgment (in Greek, epoche). Skeptics had phrases for it: “No more this than that” and “I determine nothing”. And then comes the payoff: tranquillity.

cards.headline: The painter’s sponge
cards.body: Sextus explains the payoff with a story. The painter Apelles was trying to paint the foam on a horse’s mouth and kept failing. In frustration he flung his paint-wiping sponge at the picture, and it left a perfect image of the foam. Skeptics set out to find answers, gave up, and found that calm followed anyway.

cards.headline: But how do you get out of bed?
cards.body: Critics pressed the most famous objection, the apraxia charge: without beliefs, you cannot act. Sextus replied that skeptics live by appearances. They are guided by nature, which lets them perceive and think; by feelings, as hunger leads them to food; by the customs and laws they grew up with; and by the skills they were taught.

cards.headline: The Ancient Skeptics: the big picture
learned: The apraxia charge: can a skeptic act?

questions.prompt: The Outlines of Pyrrhonism, our fullest account of Pyrrhonian skepticism, was written by _____.

options.label: Apelles the painter
options.rationale: Apelles appears in one of its stories.

options.label: Socrates
options.rationale: Socrates lived long before and wrote nothing either.

questions.explanation: Sextus Empiricus wrote it, centuries after Pyrrho, who wrote nothing.

questions.prompt: Put the skeptic’s path in order, from first step to final payoff.
items: Find an equal and opposing argument
questions.explanation: The skeptic finds an equal and opposing argument for every argument, then suspends judgment, and then comes the payoff: tranquillity.

questions.prompt: You can only know what you believe. What follows for a skeptic who suspends judgment on a question?

options.label: They know the answer more securely than others
options.rationale: Without belief, the belief leg is missing.

options.label: They know that both sides are equally true
They claim no knowledge, holding no belief
They must believe the opposite of each side

questions.explanation: Knowledge needs belief. Suspending judgment means holding no belief either way, so no claim to know.
